title: Commission decides to refer Bulgaria, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden to the Court of Justice of the European Union for failing to transpose the Directive on critical entities resilience
date_evidence: This decision was published on April 28, 2026, as document IP_26_910 on the European Commission's press corner website.
key_claim: In April 2026 the Commission referred Bulgaria, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden to the Court of Justice of the European Union, requesting financial sanctions, for failing to transpose the CER Directive whose transposition deadline was 17 October 2024.
frame_summary: The Commission frames the CJEU referral with financial sanctions as necessary enforcement of a security-critical directive that seven member states have left untransposed eighteen months after the deadline.
verbatim_quote: The European Commission decided to refer Bulgaria, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, and Sweden to the Court of Justice of the European Union for failing to transpose and notify national measures transposing the Directive on the resilience of critical entities (CER Directive).
notes: Press-corner page renders its body via JS; the referral decision and the seven member states are confirmed in the page's meta-description (verbatim_quote) captured at WebFetch. Publication date from WebSearch snippet; Clifford Chance's 15/05/2026 blog links this same URL for the referral. Body prose therefore dates the referral to April 2026 without a day-precision claim. title: Wet weerbaarheid kritieke entiteiten (36.765) — legislative dossier
date_evidence: De Eerste Kamercommissies voor Digitalisering (DIGI) en voor Justitie en Veiligheid (J&V) hebben op 2 juni 2026 het verslag (EK, B) uitgebracht en wachten op de nota naar aanleiding van het verslag.
key_claim: The Dutch Critical Entities Resilience Act (Wwke) was adopted by the Tweede Kamer on 15 April 2026 but on 2 June 2026 was still in written preparation before the Eerste Kamer, with entry into force to be set by royal decree — weeks before the 17 July 2026 designation deadline.
frame_summary: The dossier presents the Wwke as the physical-resilience twin of the Dutch Cyberbeveiligingswet implementing an EU obligation, and records without comment a legislative process still unfinished as the directive's own deadlines fall due.

title: Bundestag beschließt Gesetz zur Stärkung kritischer Anlagen (Kritis-Dachgesetz)
date_evidence: meta-date: 29.01.2026 — meta-description: Der Bundestag hat am Donnerstag, 29. Januar 2026, nach einstündiger Aussprache den Gesetzentwurf der Bundesregierung „zur Umsetzung der Richtlinie (EU) 2022 / 2557 und zur Stärkung der Resilienz kritischer Anlagen“ (Kritis-Dachgesetz, 21/2510...
key_claim: The Bundestag passed the Kritis-Dachgesetz on 29 January 2026, Germany's first cross-sector federal framework for the physical protection of critical facilities, transposing the CER Directive some fifteen months after the EU deadline; in the readings, Left-party critics argued the bill's top fine of 500,000 euros is in most cases cheaper than the protective measure itself.
frame_summary: The Bundestag record presents the Kritis-Dachgesetz as an overdue, contested first federal framework for physical critical-infrastructure protection, with opposition parties arguing its sanctions and review cycles are too weak to change operator behaviour.

title: Critical infrastructure resilience at EU-level
date_evidence: Page header shows '13 January 2026' as last page update; standing policy page maintained by DG HOME.
key_claim: The CER Directive covers eleven sectors (energy, transport, banking, financial market infrastructure, health, drinking water, wastewater, digital infrastructure, public administration, space, food); the Commission has adopted a list of essential services, run an EU-level energy-sector stress test, and issued September 2025 guidelines for identifying critical entities.
frame_summary: The Commission presents CER as one pillar of a layered EU critical-infrastructure policy — directive, stress tests, response blueprint, identification guidelines and EU-NATO cooperation — built in reaction to sabotage against European infrastructure.
verbatim_list: The protection of critical infrastructure and the resilience of critical entities operating that infrastructure are vital for modern societies.

title: The EU Critical Entities Resilience Directive: The Time to Act is Now
date_evidence: Perspective page carries no visible publication date or article:published_time metadata; treated as evergreen and cited by access date.
key_claim: EU states have until 17 July 2026 to identify critical entities, which then have ten months to comply with the resilience requirements — a window Deloitte argues is too short for the required capability build unless entities begin before designation.
frame_summary: Deloitte argues the CER timeline is ambitious enough that likely-designated entities should self-assess and build resilience capability now rather than wait for a notification letter that starts a ten-month compliance clock.
verbatim_quote: Under the CER Directive, EU states have until July 17, 2026, to identify critical entities within their respective jurisdictions and then have 10 months to comply with many new resilience requirements.
verbatim_list: Under the CER Directive, EU states have until July 17, 2026, to identify critical entities within their respective jurisdictions and then have 10 months to comply with many new resilience requirements.
Critical entities will be required to report, within 24 hours of detection, any incident that disrupts or could disrupt the provision of essential services.

title: The Netherlands Implements CER Directive: New Regime For Critical Entities
date_evidence: 15 May 2026 — visible dateline under the article title 'The Netherlands Implements CER Directive: New Regime For Critical Entities'.
key_claim: Under the Dutch Wwke, non-compliance with the duty of care and incident reporting carries fines up to the greater of EUR 10 million or 2% of worldwide turnover; the first designations are due by 17 July 2026 but depend on sectoral risk assessments that were themselves due by January 2026, so the statutory timelines have effectively converged.
frame_summary: Clifford Chance argues designation will carry consequences well beyond security compliance — cost structures, transaction planning and FDI screening — and that the Netherlands' converged statutory timelines make timely, complete designation doubtful.
verbatim_quote: Non-compliance with the duty of care and the obligation to report incidents carries the risk of administrative fines up to the greater of EUR 10 million or 2% of worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year.
verbatim_list: Non-compliance with the duty of care and the obligation to report incidents carries the risk of administrative fines up to the greater of EUR 10 million or 2% of worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year.
24 Member States had failed to meet the deadline
The proposal sets a formal deadline for the first designations of 17 July 2026, subject to the law having entered into force by that date.
Entities providing essential services in or to six or more EU Member States may additionally be assessed at EU level and designated as entities of particular European significance.
notes: Also records that entities providing essential services in or to six or more member states may be designated entities of particular European significance, and that supply chains can be ordered to exclude high-risk suppliers on national-security grounds. title: The Critical Entities Resilience Directive: Compliance Readiness Before and After July 2026
date_evidence: Article page shows only an undated 'Updated' label and no article:published_time metadata; treated as evergreen and cited by access date.
key_claim: Identification letters are expected to begin landing on corporate doorsteps in some member states during the spring and early summer of 2026, will not all arrive at once, and start a ten-month compliance clock that lands in May 2027 for entities notified on or close to the July 2026 date.
frame_summary: International SOS argues CER is a governance instrument dressed as a security one: paper compliance will fail inspection, designation letters will arrive unevenly across member states, and the binding work is rehearsed crisis decision-making rather than documentation.
verbatim_quote: Either way, in some Member States, identification letters may begin landing on corporate doorsteps during the spring and early summer of 2026.
verbatim_list: Either way, in some Member States, identification letters may begin landing on corporate doorsteps during the spring and early summer of 2026.
For those notified on or close to the July 2026 date, that lands in May 2027.
17 January 2026: Member States required to have adopted their national resilience strategy and completed their national-level risk assessment.
